Let \(f(n)\) be the last number remaining from \(\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\).  
One pass deletes positions \(1,4,7,\dots\), i.e. keeps positions \(2,3,5,6,\dots\).  
There remain \(m=\lfloor 2n/3\rfloor\) numbers, and the \(j\)-th survivor has original index \(\lceil 3j/2\rceil\). Hence
\[
f(n)=\Big\lceil \tfrac32\,f\big(\lfloor\tfrac23 n\rfloor\big)\Big\rceil,\qquad f(1)=1.
\]

Iterate the size downward:
\[
2002\to1334\to889\to592\to394\to262\to174\to116\to77\to51\to34\to22\to14\to9\to6\to4\to2\to1.
\]

Starting from \(f(1)=1\) and applying \(f(n)=\lceil \tfrac32 f(m)\rceil\) upward:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(2)&=2,\; f(4)=3,\; f(6)=5,\; f(9)=8,\; f(14)=12,\; f(22)=18,\; f(34)=27,\\
f(51)&=41,\; f(77)=62,\; f(116)=93,\; f(174)=140,\; f(262)=210,\; f(394)=315,\\
f(592)&=473,\; f(889)=710,\; f(1334)=1065,\; f(2002)=1598.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the final remaining number is \(1598\).

\boxed{1598}

Let $f(n)$ be the last remaining number when we start with $1,2,\dots,n$.  
One pass deletes positions $1,4,7,\dots$, i.e. all positions $\equiv1\pmod3$.  
The survivors are $2,3,5,6,8,9,\dots$, so there are  
$$m=n-\lceil n/3\rceil=\lfloor 2n/3\rfloor$$  
of them. The $j$-th survivor originally occupied position  
$$p(j)=\Big\lfloor\frac{3j+1}{2}\Big\rfloor.$$  
Hence $f(1)=1$ and for $n>1$,
$$f(n)=\Big\lfloor\frac{3\,f(\lfloor 2n/3\rfloor)+1}{2}\Big\rfloor.$$

Applying this repeatedly for $n=2002$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
2002&\to1334\to889\to592\to394\to262\to174\to116\\
&\to77\to51\to34\to22\to14\to9\to6\to4\to2\to1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting $f(1)=1$:
$f(2)=2$, $f(4)=3$, $f(6)=5$, $f(9)=8$, $f(14)=12$, $f(22)=18$, $f(34)=27$, $f(51)=41$, $f(77)=62$, $f(116)=93$, $f(174)=140$, $f(262)=210$, $f(394)=315$, $f(592)=473$, $f(889)=710$, $f(1334)=1065$, and finally
$$f(2002)=\Big\lfloor\frac{3\cdot1065+1}{2}\Big\rfloor=1598.$$

(Direct simulation of the erasure process on $1,\dots,2002$ also yields $1598$.)
